rv.q: Director Will Blum creates an exciting energy with this cast with moments hurtling by, taking us to a denouement that just makes perfect sense.
Still, it holds your interest and, at an hour and 15 minutes (a bit longer than a TV episode), gives you something to talk about on the way to the subway.

But she’s up against Suarez, a clever defense attorney with political connections who seems intent on painting this as a case of racial profiling (the defendant is named “Herman Crespo,” but officer Sampson refers to him as “the spic”). Suarez knows how to get the cops off-script to discredit their testimony.

Yet, whether or not one agrees with the show’s worldview, the production that is opening tonight at AMT Theater is ultimately unpersuasive as a pointed slice-of-life legal drama, because some missteps both undermine its verisimilitude and lessen its dramatic impact.

cn.t: A gritty cop drama from a defense attorney-playwright draws mixed reviews—critics find it fierce and authentic but also flawed and overly familiar in its exploration of police corruption and the criminal justice system.
